Today in Canada you can expect to live longer than your
great-grandparents. This was not always the case. In the past,
many people died from widespread outbreaks of disease.
What causes disease? How does disease spread? How does the
body protect itself from disease? How do the characteristics
you inherit from your parents affect your health? How does
the environment influence health?
For centuries, scientists have searched for
answers to all of these questions. They discovered
that disease-causing agents spread disease. In this
unit you will learn about disease-carrying agents
such as Giardia, which is present in water.
Today, antibiotics treat many diseases
successfully. Research about how characteristics
are passed from parent to child helps us better
understand inherited diseases.
In this unit you will learn about all of these
things, and about how public health helps to keep
us all healthier than our great-grandparents.
Knowledge about these topics can benefit your
life in many ways.

Causes of Human Disease

Why do people get sick? In the past, people
thought diseases were caused by various spirits or
gods. Some people still hold these ideas. Scientists
have another theory.
Disease, or illness, prevents the normal  
functioning of the body. As a result of the invention 
of 
the microscope, scientists like Louis Pasteur and 
Robert Koch found and identified micro-organisms  
known as microbes . The microbes that cause disease 
are called pathogens or germs.
Pathogens are not the only things that cause 
disease. Some diseases are caused by a poor 
environment. For example, air pollution can damage 
the lungs. 
Other diseases are genetic; for example, muscular 
dystrophy. This disease causes progressive weakness 
of the muscles.
Disease may also arise from a combination of 
factors that include the environment, diet, lifestyle, 
genetics, pathogens, and stress. For example, have 
you ever noticed how often you get sick when you 
are worried about a relationship? Often, when people 
are stressed, they eat poorly and may stop exercising. 
The diet and lifestyle choices they make combine 
with stress to make them more likely to get sick.
Pathogens live in toilets, air conditioners, and 
dirty wash cloths. If these are not cleaned regularly, 
the number of pathogens may increase. Indoor and 
outdoor pollutants can affect your health to a greater 
or lesser degree, depending on the type and amount 
of pollutants and your sensitivity to them.

Viruses
Like bacteria, viruses can be found anywhere there are cells to infect — and you are made of trillions of 
such cells.
Viruses, such as the common cold virus, are much smaller than 
bacteria. They reproduce by taking over cells in the body. V iruses use 
the part of the body cell usually used to reproduce cells. In this way, the 
number of viruses quickly multiplies, and they invade other body cells.
Pathogens
Pathogens are disease-causing microbes. Most pathogens are 
microscopic. These include some bacteria, viruses, fungi, and 
protists.
Bacteria
Bacteria are on your skin, in your mouth, in the air you breathe, and 
in the food you eat. Why can’t you see them? Because they are single-
celled organisms so small that you need a microscope to see one.
Some bacteria are beneficial to humans. Yogurt, for example, is 
made from milk and a bacterium that causes milk to go sour. 
Other bacteria are harmful to humans. They cause disease and
spoil food.

and form colonies when conditions are good. The box below shows

Protists
Protists are single-celled organisms that share some characteristics
with both animals and plants. Two common protists are the
amoeba and the paramecium.
Some protists cause serious diseases such as malaria, African
sleeping sickness, and amoebic dysentery. Malaria is spread by
mosquitoes, sleeping sickness by Tsetse flies. Amoeba can be
picked up from contaminated water or food.
A protist called Giardia lives in the intestines of infected
humans or animals. Gi ardia may be found in water, food, soil, or
surfaces that have been contaminated with the feces from infected
humans or animals. You can become infected after you drink the 
contaminated water.
To prevent getting Giardia, drink only safe water. 
Fungi
Fungi include molds, yeasts, and 
mushrooms. They cannot make 
their own food by photosynthesis. 
Some fungi are parasites and can 
live only on host organisms. Fungi, 
such as mushrooms taste great on 
pizza or salad. Others cause disease. 
Two examples of this are athlete’s 
foot and ringworm, two fungi that 
live on the body.

You can catch a cold from a friend, but can you get diabetes from one?
The answer is no. You can catch a cold from someone because a cold is a
communicable disease. Colds are caused by pathogens that can spread from
one person to another.
But diabetes is a non-communicable disease. It is not caused by a
pathogen. Such diseases cannot spread from person to person.

The diseases are communicable because the pathogen carrying the
disease 
can spread from one organism to another. The flu, the
common cold, 
and AIDS are all examples of communicable diseases.

The Importance of a Clean Environment 
Diseases can be spread by air, water, food, and contact. Why aren’t we all sick
most of the time?
The answer has to do with our environment. Clean environments reduce the
number of viruses and bacteria present. As a result, there are fewer pathogens
to make us sick.
Some environments have to be super clean. There are so many pathogens 
associated with human feces that bathrooms have to be sanitary. This means 
maintaining clean, germ-free conditions to help prevent disease. This form of 
cleaning uses special cleaners such as chlorine and anti-bacterial soaps to eliminate 
most bacteria and viruses. Sanitary cleaning and handling practices should be used 
in all environments where there is a chance of high numbers of bacteria and viruses.
People who work with food must wear protective gloves when they are handling
food, to avoid spreading pathogens to people who will eat the food they serve.
Another reason they need to handle food carefully is to prevent food poisoning.
Food poisoning results from eating food that is infected with harmful micro-
organisms. Such food can make you very ill. In some cases, it can be fatal.

Who Is Most Likely 
to Get Sick?
In Canada, the average female can expect to live 81 years. The average male will likely see his 75th 
birthday. In Sierra 
Leone, an African country, the average female will live only 35 years and the average 
male 33 
years. The difference has to do with living conditions.
Canada is a wealthy country. Most Canadians have enough food, clean water
to drink, air that is relatively unpolluted, proper health care, and access to public
education. The majority of adult Canadians also have paying jobs.
People in Sierra Leone have access to few or none of these 
things. In short, they 
live in poverty. This means that their basic  
needs for food, water, health care, and education are not met.
Children born in poor countries often die of starvation. They 
are also more likely to get a communicable disease. Because there 
is little health care, they often die from such illnesses.
Those who do survive to adulthood continue to be more likely
to get a communicable disease. In Canada, pollution-control
plants purify drinking water. In poor countries, drinking water
comes directly from streams and rivers, which may be full of
bacteria, viruses, and parasites.

frequently,

Keeping Hospitals Healthy
Two hundred years ago, people expected to die when 
they went 
to the hospital. Hospitals were so unsanitary 
that patients often picked up diseases in the hospital. 
Today, this is less common because of the work of 
scientists such as Florence Nightingale, Joseph Lister, 
and Robert Koch.
In the 1800s, Florence Nightingale worked in a military 
hospital in Turkey. She reduced the death rate by making 
sure the hospital and patients were kept clean, improving 
water quality, and bandaging wounds to prevent infections 
from spreading to other patients.
Around the same time, an English surgeon named 
Joseph 
Lister realized that many patients died of infections 
following surgery. He began spraying carbolic acid on 
patient wounds and into the air of operating theatres. 
Carbolic 
acid kills pathogens on surfaces and on skin.
Robert Koch discovered that hot steam was effective in 
killing pathogens. He began using steam to destroy living 
organisms. This process is called
 sterilization.

Aseptic Methods
Modern medicine uses many techniques to keep hospital rooms  
and equipment aseptic or free of pathogens. Aseptic practices 
include: 
•using sterile bandages, instruments, linens, masks, and
clothing during surgery;
•scrubbing all exposed skin of the surgeon before and after
surgery;
•having surgical staff wear rubber gloves to prevent the
spread of pathogens that might hide under fingernails.
In addition, antiseptics are used on people to disinfect the skin.
Such antiseptics include iodine solution and alcohol.
Disinfectants are used on objects and surfaces to sterilize them. 
Some common disinfectants include iodine, chlorine, bleach, and 
antibacterial soaps.

Allergies
Allergies develop when the immune system overreacts and becomes sensitive to
substances such as pollen, dust, or mould. The immune system then treats the
substance as though it were a pathogen and begins to build antibodies against
it. These antibodies result in a variety of symptoms. Mild reactions include a
runny nose and itchy or watery eyes. Severe symptoms can include breathing
difficulties, and can build to extreme allergic reactions that cause death.
Scratch tests identify allergens. Drops of antigen are absorbed under the
scratched skin. Allergic reactions produce redness, swelling, and itching along
the scratch.
People who suffer from allergies sometimes get immunotherapy. This
involves injections of weakened allergens. Regular injections build the number
of antibodies against the allergen.

Recording Inherited Traits
Since chromosomes come in pairs, genes for traits do too. Many traits are
controlled by only one pair of genes, others by two or more pairs.
For traits controlled by one pair of genes, geneticists use two letters to
represent the genotype or combination of genes.
• Capital letters represent dominant genes. For example, the letter T could
represent the dominant gene for tallness, which is the tall gene.
• Lower case letter represent recessive genes. For example, the letter t could
represent the recessive gene for tallness.
During reproduction, chromosomes separate so that each sperm or egg cell
gets only one chromosome of each kind. As a result, only one gene for each
trait is passed on to the offspring from each parent.

Genetic Changes
Most of the time the process of cell reproduction and copying genes works
well. Mistakes, however, can happen during reproduction when chromosomes
are copied. In most cases, body cells recognize errors and fix them. In other
cases, a cell’s repair mechanisms can fail. These mistakes are then passed from
generation to generation. 
Such changes in genetic information can result in an abnormal gene called 
a mutation. Mutations can occur in several ways. Figure 12.7 shows how the 
change in one of the base pairs of a gene can lead to sickle-cell anemia.
Exposure to environmental factors can also cause mutations. Environmental 
factors that cause mutations are called mutagens. These include radiation; 
ultraviolet light; and many chemicals, including PCBs, those in cigarettes, and 
alcohol and other drugs.
Most of these errors do not pass from one generation to the next. There are
exceptions. For example, children may pass on some effects from their mother’s
exposure to radiation.
Inherited Genetic Disorders
Sometimes, a mutation may be helpful. For example, giraffes with a mutation 
for a longer neck increase their ability to obtain food. Usually mutations result 
in genetic disorders, which result from alterations to the genes. For example, 
sickle cell anemia results from an abnormal form of hemoglobin. Hemoglobin 
is the substance in red blood cells that carries oxygen through the body. 
Someone with sickle cell anemia has abnormal hemoglobin. This leads to poor 
resistance to infection and low levels of iron in the blood.

What would happen if all parents decided to have only male — or only female —
children? This is the kind of question people ask when discussing genetic research.
Such questions are ethical questions. They consider what is right or wrong.
Some ethical concerns deal with questions about who should have access to
genetic information. For example, might employers ask for genetic information
about employees? How might they use it?

• Who has a right to genetic data that provide information about your
